guide.title: Patients with Special Challenges
guide.lead: Disability, mental illness, sensory loss, language, poverty and home medical technology change how you assess and communicate, not what the patient deserves. Ask what is normal for them, look for the medical cause behind a change in behaviour, and use the expertise of whoever lives with the device.

sections.title: Communicating
rows: Face them in good light and ask how they communicate. Write, type, or use a qualified sign language interpreter (in person or video). Don't shout; don't use children to interpret.
Say who you are; explain before touching; describe the surroundings; offer your arm. Keep the guide dog with them.
A professional interpreter by phone or video. Speak to the patient in short sentences. Family only for urgent basics.
Quiet, low light, few people. Explain each step before you do it and give time. Ask carers how pain shows; let them keep comfort items.
Speak to the patient first, in plain words; check understanding. Carers know the baseline.
Introduce yourself each time; one question at a time; calm voice.

sections.title: Behaviour change: medical first?
sections.question: Abnormal glucose, SpO₂, temperature or vital signs; new confusion; injury; toxins or a change in medicines?
sections.yes: Treat it as medical. Hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, sepsis, head injury, pain and drug toxicity (lithium, anticholinergics) all look 'behavioural'.
sections.no: De-escalate: your name, their name, calm voice, real choices, safe distance and an exit. Restraint only as a last resort, per protocol, never face-down.

sections.title: Technology at home
rows: DOPE: Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment. Oxygen to the face and stoma; suction to the pre-measured depth for under 15 seconds; change the inner tube. Still blocked: replace the tube (same size or one smaller), or ventilate via the stoma or by mask over the face with the stoma covered.
Disconnect and ventilate by bag through the trach with oxygen. Bring the ventilator and its settings.
Headache, vomiting, drowsiness, irritability, bulging fontanelle: neurosurgical centre.
Cover the site and bring the tube: the tract starts to close within hours.
Pressure for bleeding; clamp a broken line; fever with a line is sepsis until proven otherwise.
There may be no palpable pulse: judge by mental state and skin. Listen for the pump hum, call the coordinator number on the device, follow their advice on compressions.
No BP, IV or tight dressing on that arm. Bleeding: firm pressure. Missed dialysis: high potassium, fluid overload.
Suspend or disconnect the pump, then treat the glucose.

groups.title: Down syndrome
items: Atlantoaxial instability: careful with the neck
Heart disease, early dementia, low thyroid

groups.title: Homelessness and poverty
items: Cold and heat injury, infections, wounds, TB, untreated chronic disease, substance use
Treat with dignity; ask what would make hospital easier

groups.title: Capacity to refuse
items: Can they understand, retain and weigh the information, and communicate a choice?
Sepsis, hypoxia, head injury and intoxication can remove capacity

items.label: Hyperkalemia
items.sub: Missed dialysis: peaked T waves, then wide QRS. Treat before arrest.

quiz.q: Non-verbal 5-year-old with autism: crying, pulling at his ears, hitting his head. Consider first:
options: Pain or illness, such as an ear infection
quiz.explanation: Behaviour is how many autistic children show pain.

quiz.q: Man with schizophrenia: agitated and confused; BP 88/56, SpO₂ 91%, glucose 42 mg/dL. Most likely cause?
quiz.explanation: Check glucose in every patient with altered behaviour.

quiz.q: 42-year-old with Down syndrome after a minor crash has midline neck tenderness. Priority?
options: Spinal motion restriction: atlantoaxial instability is possible
Clear the neck because the crash was minor

quiz.q: Best approach to a blind patient:
options: Say who you are and explain before touching
Guide them silently by the arm
quiz.explanation: Describe the surroundings and offer your arm.

quiz.q: Homeless man asleep outside at 2 °C: confused, cold, mottled, shivering. You:
options: Treat as hypothermia and transport; look for injury, infection, alcohol and low glucose
Give a blanket and leave him
Call police for a welfare check only
Give hot coffee and walk him

quiz.q: Dialysis patient with a left-arm fistula needs an IV. Where?
options: The left arm, above the fistula
quiz.explanation: No BP, IV or blood draws on the fistula arm.

quiz.q: 22-year-old autistic man with asthma pulls off his mask; SpO₂ 89%, diffuse wheeze. Mother says he's just scared. You:
options: Explain it's a real emergency, reduce stimulation, explain each step, involve his mother, continue treatment and transport
quiz.explanation: Hypoxia and fear both drive his agitation.

quiz.q: Deaf patient who uses sign language; her mother offers to interpret. Best?
options: A qualified interpreter (in person or video); write in the meantime
quiz.explanation: Family interpreters filter and miss details.

quiz.q: Child with a tracheostomy is in distress and you hear gurgling. First?
options: Oxygen and suction the tube to its pre-measured depth

quiz.q: Capacity to refuse care needs the patient to:
options: Understand, retain and weigh the information, and communicate a choice
quiz.explanation: Sepsis or hypoxia can remove capacity.

flashcards.question: Autism: EMS approach
flashcards.answer: May be non-verbal or use devices. Reduce light, noise and touch; explain each step; allow time; ask carers about baseline and pain. Don't assume they don't understand.

flashcards.question: Down syndrome: atlantoaxial instability
flashcards.answer: Some people with Down syndrome have an unstable C1–C2 joint. Handle the neck carefully in trauma and airway management.

flashcards.question: De-escalation
flashcards.answer: Calm voice, use their name, acknowledge feelings, give real choices, don't argue with delusions, keep distance and an exit. Check for medical causes first.

flashcards.question: Deaf or hard of hearing
flashcards.answer: Face them in good light, write or type, use a qualified interpreter. Normal voice – don't shout. Don't use children to interpret.

flashcards.question: Using an interpreter
flashcards.answer: Professional, not family. Speak to the patient, not the interpreter; short sentences; allow time.

flashcards.question: AV fistula
flashcards.answer: No BP, IV or blood draws on that arm: it can clot the access. Bleeding: firm direct pressure.

flashcards.question: Aggressive or self-injuring autistic patient
flashcards.answer: Consider pain or illness. Reduce stimulation, simple calm language, assess for injury, ask carers, transport if needed.

flashcards.question: Medical first
flashcards.answer: New behaviour may be hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, infection, head injury or drug toxicity. Check vital signs and glucose in everyone.

critical.scenario: Group home: 28-year-old with autism and intellectual disability, hitting his head, shouting, rocking; flushed, warm, breathing fast. Known seizures. Staff say he just needs to be left alone.
critical.question: Priority?

options.t: Look for a medical cause: vital signs, glucose, temperature, injury, post-ictal state; reduce stimulation; transport if he can't be assessed safely

options.f: Fever and fast breathing need assessment.

critical.explanation: Fever plus behaviour change can be infection or meningitis.
critical.kpi: Looks for medical causes of behavioural change

critical.scenario: 45-year-old on lithium for bipolar disorder: confused, slurred speech, unsteady, a week of feeling worse and 2 days of vomiting and diarrhoea. Nurse thinks it's mania. BP 100/62, HR 108, glucose normal.
critical.question: Most likely cause?

options.t: Lithium toxicity worsened by dehydration: medical emergency, IV fluids per protocol, transport

options.f: Ataxia and GI symptoms point to toxicity.

critical.explanation: Vomiting and diarrhoea reduce lithium clearance; so do NSAIDs, diuretics and ACE inhibitors.
critical.kpi: Recognizes lithium toxicity presenting as altered mental status

critical.scenario: Homeless man with a swollen, red, foul-smelling shin wound and blisters to the knee; fever, HR 112, confused. Smells of alcohol. Refuses: 'I'll clean it with whiskey.'
critical.question: How do you handle the refusal?

options.t: Explain the risk plainly, address his worries (belongings, friends), assess capacity – confusion from sepsis may remove it – and involve medical direction and police per protocol
He's talking, so accept the refusal

options.f: Only with lack of capacity and legal authority.

critical.explanation: Document capacity, information given and who you consulted.
critical.kpi: Assesses decision-making capacity in a septic patient refusing care
